title: The Argument from the Big Bang
short: the Big Bang and a beginning of the universe

keyTerms.d: A modern, scientifically informed version of an old argument — named for the medieval Islamic theologians who sharpened it, and revived in our day above all by William Lane Craig. In its cleanest form it has three lines: whatever begins to exist has a cause; the universe began to exist; therefore the universe has a cause.

The deliberate wording of Premise 1 — not “everything has a cause.” The theist does not claim God needs a cause; the claim is about things that come into being, and a being that never began to exist is simply not in the argument’s scope. Nearly every careless version of the argument stumbles here.

The standard model of cosmology: the expansion and cooling of the universe from an extremely hot, dense early state. It rests on a convergence of independent lines — cosmic expansion, the microwave background, and the light-element abundances — that were never designed to test anyone’s theology, and it is accepted across the field regardless of metaphysics.

The point of infinite density predicted when general relativity is extrapolated all the way back. It is widely regarded by physicists as a signal that the theory has broken down, not a photograph of the first instant. The singularity theorems establish a boundary to the classical spacetime, not a literal point of zero size.

Using only the assumption that a universe has, on average, been expanding throughout its history, it shows that the spacetime cannot be extended infinitely into the past — it must have a past boundary. It requires no assumption about matter or energy conditions, so it applies even to inflationary and many multiverse models. It is a result about classical spacetime, and its co-author Alan Guth suspects the universe did not begin — so it is powerful corroboration, not proof.

keyTerms.t: Inference to the best explanation (evidence, not proof)
keyTerms.d: The deliberately modest epistemic status of the case. The argument does not need cosmology to be finished; it needs only that, weighing the convergence of evidence against the alternatives, a real beginning is more reasonable than its denial — offered for examination, not as a demonstration that forecloses inquiry.

The metaphysical intuition that grounds Premise 1: things do not spring into being from literal non-being, uncaused, for no reason. If they could, it becomes inexplicable why we do not constantly observe anything and everything popping into existence. The uniform causal track record of science supports it, with one honest limit — that record is of causes rearranging pre-existing material within time.

keyTerms.t: A transcendent cause, not yet the Triune God
keyTerms.d: The bounded reach of the argument. The cause of all space and time cannot itself be spatial or temporal; it must be transcendent, immaterial, uncaused and immensely powerful — a sketch that converges remarkably with classical theism. But by physics alone it does not reach the God of the Nicene Creed; getting to the Father, Son and Holy Spirit needs the further resources of natural theology and, above all, the historical evidence for the resurrection.

derive.q: Does Premise 1 say “everything has a cause”…?
derive.ans: no — only whatever BEGINS to exist has a cause
derive.why: The theist does not claim God needs a cause; the claim is about things that come into being, and a being that never began to exist is simply not in the argument’s scope. Stating it as “everything has a cause” invites the schoolyard reply “then who caused God?” — which the careful wording never licenses.

derive.q: The Big Bang shows expansion from a hot, dense early state — so does that by itself prove the absolute first moment of all reality…?
derive.ans: no — it is evidence for Premise 2, not proof of theism
derive.why: The standard model describes the expansion and cooling of the universe from a hot, dense early state; it does not, by itself, prove that this was the first moment of all reality. The singularity is widely read as where general relativity breaks down, not a photograph of the first instant. Classical physics points to a beginning; what a future theory of quantum gravity will say is not yet settled.

derive.q: BGV needs no energy conditions, only average expansion — so what does its past boundary establish, and what not…?
derive.ans: a classical past boundary — strong corroboration, not proof
derive.why: It is a kinematic result about expansion as such, which is why it reaches inflationary and many multiverse models. But it is a result about classical spacetime, and the regime it reaches is where quantum gravity would take over; its own co-author Alan Guth suspects the universe did not begin. So it corroborates that the cosmologies we can write down run into a past boundary — evidence, not a demonstration that being itself began.

derive.q: Grant that the universe began — why think it had a cause…?
derive.ans: out of nothing, nothing comes, and the causal record is robust
derive.why: Things do not spring from literal non-being uncaused; if they could, it is inexplicable why we do not see anything and everything doing so constantly. The causal principle is among the most robustly confirmed we have. Honest limit: that record is entirely of causes rearranging pre-existing material within time, so at the absolute beginning it is the metaphysical intuition, not the inductive record, that carries the weight — a reasonable warrant, not a proof.

derive.q: The analysis reaches a transcendent, powerful cause — is that the God of the Nicene Creed…?
derive.ans: no — a transcendent, immaterial, powerful cause, not yet the Triune God
derive.why: A cause of all space and time cannot be spatial or temporal; it must be immaterial, immensely powerful and uncaused. That converges remarkably with classical theism, and strikingly it falls out of the analysis rather than being smuggled in. But to get from a First Cause to the Father Almighty one needs natural theology and, finally, revelation — above all the historical evidence for the resurrection.

honestState.p1: The hot Big Bang model itself — expansion, the microwave background, the light-element abundances — is not in serious dispute; it is the standard model of cosmology, accepted across the field regardless of metaphysics. What is disputed is the metaphysical interpretation of the past boundary: whether it is a true beginning of being, or the place where our physics runs out and a deeper theory might continue the story. Alexander Vilenkin reads the evidence as favouring a beginning; Sean Carroll and Alan Guth — a co-author of the BGV theorem — both lean against a beginning while granting that nobody knows; many cosmologists regard it as simply unsettled pending a theory of quantum gravity we do not yet have. The live literature is real and technical: cyclic and bouncing models (Steinhardt and Turok; Ijjas and Steinhardt) answered by Kinney and Stein, and defended again by Pavlović and Sossich; the past-completeness argument of Lesnefsky, Easson and Davies (2023); and the philosophical challenges of Daniel Linford and Phillip Halper. None of these is a fringe position.
honestState.fairness: Honest defenders concede the observations. The singularity is widely regarded as a sign general relativity has broken down, not a photograph of the first instant. Even the BGV theorem is a classical result, and its most famous co-author, Alan Guth, suspects the universe did not begin — very likely eternal, though nobody knows. Genuine loopholes remain on the table: contracting-phase bounce models, which Vilenkin himself judged “essentially equivalent to a beginning,” and a multiverse scenario he explored with Garriga where the theorem “may not apply.” The “universe from nothing” proposals target a real ambiguity in the word. And the causal principle’s uniform track record is entirely of causes rearranging pre-existing material within time, so extending it to the absolute beginning is a step a thoughtful critic can resist. But the inference does not follow: this is a convergence argument, and the proposed escapes either smuggle in a structured “something,” or face thermodynamic and BGV-type pressure, or remain speculative. As an argument that the universe did not begin, none of them holds.
honestState.verdict: So our own claim is deliberately modest, and we make it plainly: the best current science is consistent with — indeed naturally suggestive of — a universe with a finite past. That is an inference to the best explanation about the physics, offered for examination, not a demonstration. A universe that began is better explained by a transcendent cause beyond it than by no cause at all — a bounded yes: the Big Bang does not prove God, and it commits the Christian to no reading of Genesis and to no side in the old-earth / young-earth debate, which are weighed on other grounds. The cause it points to is transcendent, immaterial, uncaused and immensely powerful — a real pointer toward a Creator, though not, by itself, to the Triune God of the Nicene Creed. Reaching that God needs natural theology and, above all, the historical evidence for the resurrection.

The universe began to exist — the best current cosmology is naturally suggestive of a finite past: evidence, not proof.
Therefore the universe has a cause — a transcendent cause beyond space and time, inferred rather than proven, and not yet the Triune God.

cards.q: What are the two points of precision that keep this argument honest?
cards.a: First, Premise 1 says “whatever begins to exist has a cause,” not “everything has a cause” — God never began, so is not in the argument’s scope. Second, the conclusion is modest: it yields a cause, not yet a God. The Big Bang is evidence for Premise 2, not a proof of theism by itself.

cards.q: What three independent lines of evidence converge on a hot, dense early state?
cards.a: Cosmic expansion (galaxies recede at speeds proportional to their distance), the cosmic microwave background (the cooled-down relic of an early hot state, predicted before it was detected), and the predicted abundances of the lightest elements. No single observation carries the weight — none was designed to test anyone’s theology.

cards.q: What does the initial singularity actually mark?
cards.a: The point of infinite density predicted when general relativity is run all the way back — widely regarded as a signal the theory has broken down, not a photograph of the first instant. The singularity theorems establish a boundary to the classical spacetime, not a literal zero. Classical physics points to a beginning; what quantum gravity will say is not yet settled.

cards.q: What does the Borde–Guth–Vilenkin theorem establish, and on what single assumption?
cards.a: Using only that a universe has on average been expanding, it shows the spacetime cannot be extended infinitely into the past — it must have a past boundary — with no assumption about matter or energy conditions. That is why it reaches inflationary and many multiverse models, which were its authors’ original target.

cards.q: Why is the BGV theorem “evidence, not proof”?
cards.a: It is a result about classical spacetime, and the regime it reaches back into is exactly where quantum gravity would take over; and its own co-author Alan Guth suspects the universe did not begin — very likely eternal, though nobody knows. So it is powerful corroboration that the cosmologies we can write down run into a past boundary, not a demonstration that being itself began.

cards.q: What does Vilenkin’s “no models at this time” line claim — and what does it not claim?
cards.a: Reviewing the leading models with Mithani in 2012, Vilenkin found none that is genuinely past-eternal and said there are “no models at this time that provide a satisfactory model for a universe without a beginning.” Note the careful phrase “at this time”: that is a report on the present state of the models, not a closed book.

cards.q: How does the “a universe from nothing” objection fail?
cards.a: David Albert’s point: a law-governed quantum vacuum is emphatically something — a structured physical reality, not non-being — and the stronger, no-vacuum version still presupposes quantum laws and a wave function. Calling that apparatus “nothing” changes the meaning of the word; the question merely retreats to where the law-governed substrate came from.

cards.q: How do cyclic / bouncing models try to stay eternal, and where does the pressure bite?
cards.a: They replace the singularity with a bounce and answer Tolman’s 1934 entropy objection by diluting entropy as the universe grows from cycle to cycle. But a universe that grows on balance is expanding on average — the one thing BGV needs — and Steinhardt and Turok judged “the most likely story” for their earlier model was a singular beginning. Contested territory, not a closed case.

cards.q: Does eternal inflation or the multiverse remove the beginning?
cards.a: No — that was the very scenario BGV was written to address: because the inflating background expands on average, it too must have a past boundary in its classical description. The multiverse relocates the beginning one level up rather than dissolving it, though Vilenkin flagged a scenario with Garriga where the theorem “may not apply,” and Lesnefsky, Easson and Davies (2023) argue some inflationary spacetimes may be past-complete.

cards.q: Why is the defence of Premise 1 honest about its own limits?
cards.a: Its warrant is the intuition that out of nothing, nothing comes, plus the robust causal track record — but that record is entirely of causes rearranging pre-existing material within time. Extending the principle to the absolute beginning, where there is no prior material and no prior moment, is a step a thoughtful critic can resist; there it is the metaphysical intuition, not induction, that carries the weight.

cards.q: What does analysing the cause yield — and where does the analysis stop?
cards.a: A cause of all space and time cannot be spatial or temporal; it must be immaterial, immensely powerful and uncaused on pain of regress. That converges remarkably with classical theism — but it is not yet the full God of the Nicene Creed. Craig’s further step, that the cause is plausibly personal (a timeless cause of a temporal effect points to a free agent), is a disputed philosophical inference, not a result of physics.

cards.q: What is the bounded answer to the title question?
cards.a: A bounded yes: the Big Bang does not prove God, but a universe that began is better explained by a transcendent cause beyond it than by no cause at all — a real pointer toward a Creator, though not, by itself, to the Triune God. It also takes no side between old-earth and young-earth readings; identifying that cause with the God revealed in Christ is the work of revelation, above all the resurrection.

obj.q: Sean Carroll, debating Craig in 2014, pressed the point: the BGV theorem is about classical spacetime descriptions, and the regime it reaches back into is precisely where classical descriptions fail and quantum gravity takes over. A “past boundary” in the classical model need not be a metaphysical beginning of being — it may simply mark where our current equations stop applying. And “beginning” and even “cause,” he argues, are not fundamental features of physics at all but emergent, macroscopic notions ill-suited to the boundary of spacetime.
obj.model: That limit has to be stated as plainly as the theorem’s strength, and it is true: BGV is a classical result, and the boundary it finds is exactly where a quantum-gravity description would take over. What that leaves is a genuine dispute about how to interpret the past boundary — whether it is a true beginning of being, or the place where our physics runs out and a deeper theory might continue the story. And the field divides honestly here: Vilenkin reads the evidence as favouring a beginning; Carroll and Guth both lean against while granting that nobody knows; many cosmologists regard it as simply unsettled pending a theory of quantum gravity we do not yet have — none of these a fringe position. But the argument does not need cosmology to be finished. It needs only that, weighing the convergence of evidence against the alternatives, a real beginning is more reasonable than its denial. So the objection does not defeat the case; what it correctly establishes is the bound we already place on it — this is evidence and an inference to the best explanation, not proof, and never a claim that physics has demonstrated a Creator.

obj.q: In A Universe from Nothing (2012) Lawrence Krauss argued that quantum field theory lets a universe arise spontaneously from the vacuum, so no creator is required; at its strongest, he argues that quantum gravity may allow even space and time themselves to arise, with no pre-existing vacuum at all. So the something-from-nothing problem the argument trades on simply dissolves.
obj.model: The trouble is the word “nothing,” and the sharpest critic is not a theologian but the philosopher of physics David Albert, who reviewed the book for the New York Times. Albert observed that relativistic quantum fields are emphatically something: “if what we formerly took for nothing turns out, on closer examination, to have the makings of protons and neutrons and tables and chairs and planets and solar systems and galaxies and universes in it, then it wasn’t nothing.” A quantum vacuum governed by laws is a structured physical reality, not non-being; and the stronger, no-vacuum version still presupposes quantum laws, a wave function, the mathematical structure that does the “creating.” The question merely retreats one step: where did the quantum substrate and the laws governing it come from? So the objection does not show the universe needs no cause — it trades on a shift in the meaning of “nothing,” and it relocates the question rather than answering it. (That is a point about preservation of the puzzle, not yet a proof of theism.)

obj.q: A bounce keeps the universe past-eternal — contracting, rebounding, and expanding again without end. Modern cyclic models answer Richard Tolman’s 1934 entropy objection: Steinhardt and Turok dilute entropy by an exponential factor each cycle so that only the entropy density, “which is all any real observer would actually see,” behaves cyclically, and Ijjas and Steinhardt’s “New Kind of Cyclic Universe” has the scale factor grow exponentially from one cycle to the next, so the universe “can undergo an unbounded number of cycles in the past.” This is serious physics, and Tolman’s 1934 objection does not settle the matter against it.
obj.model: Granted — and the strongest form of the model deserves that hearing. But the second pressure is where it bites: the entropy is diluted because the universe grows from cycle to cycle, and a universe that grows on balance is expanding on average — the one assumption the BGV theorem needs. On William Kinney and Nina Stein’s analysis, answering Tolman that way walks straight into BGV, and that worry is not merely an apologist’s gloss: asked of their own earlier model, “Does this mean that the cycling has no beginning?”, Steinhardt and Turok answered, “This issue is not settled at present,” and judged that “the most likely story is that cycling was preceded by some singular beginning.” The loophole is genuine and I will not hide it — Pavlović and Sossich claim a class of geodesically complete cyclic models, and BGV is itself a classical result whose co-author Guth suspects no beginning. So the verdict is bounded: the cyclic escape has not been refuted, but its best-known answer to the entropy problem trades that difficulty for another, and its own architects judged a beginning the most likely story. It is a live hypothesis, not a demonstration that the past is eternal.

obj.q: Grant that the universe began. Your causal principle is only ever confirmed for causes rearranging pre-existing material within space and time — you have never once observed anything come into being from literal non-being. Extending the principle to the absolute beginning of the universe itself, where there is no prior material and no prior moment, is an unwarranted leap, and the whole argument turns on that leap.
obj.model: That concession is exactly right, and an honest defender grants it outright: the inductive track record is entirely of causes rearranging pre-existing material within time, so extending it to the absolute beginning is a step a thoughtful critic can resist. But notice what the defence rests on at that point — not the inductive record, but the metaphysical intuition that out of nothing, nothing comes: things do not spring into being from non-being, uncaused, for no reason. And that intuition is not idle: if things could come from literal non-being uncaused, it becomes inexplicable why we do not constantly observe anything and everything popping into existence. So the limb is conceded in full and the argument is bounded accordingly — Premise 1 at the beginning is carried by a metaphysical intuition rather than by induction, which is a serious and reasonable warrant, not a knock-down proof. That is why the conclusion is offered as an inference to the best explanation, not a demonstration.

unseen.q: Grant the whole cosmology — the expansion, the background glow, the light elements, even a finite past. You still cannot say the Big Bang supports the Christian doctrine of creation. Consonance is not support: a universe created in time would, from our vantage point, look much as the cosmologists’ Big Bang does — but that is a long way from the physics confirming the doctrine, and the inference should be refused in both directions.
unseen.model: The distinction is real and this essay keeps it: consonance is not proof, and the cosmology does not, by itself, establish the doctrine of creation out of nothing. It commits the Christian to no particular reading of Genesis and to no side in the old-earth / young-earth debate, which are weighed on other grounds. But McMullin’s refusal goes further than the evidence requires: an observation that is more to be expected if the universe is created than if it is not does count in that doctrine’s favour, if only modestly. So the claim defended here is only the modest one — that a finite past is more reasonable than its denial, an inference to the best explanation about the physics rather than a deductive proof, and that such a beginning is the kind of thing one would expect if the universe is created. It is a real pointer toward a Creator, not a demonstration, and not by itself the God of the Nicene Creed.
